grammar: 배고파요 (baegopayo = I'm hungry) — no pronoun needed; Korean drops "I".
안 before the verb = didn't: 안 먹었어요 (an meogeosseoyo = didn't eat).
점심 먹었어요? (jeomsim meogeosseoyo) doubles as a friendly greeting, like "how's it going?"
목말라요 (mongmallayo = I'm thirsty) — 목 (throat) + 마르다 (to be dry).

english: There are lots of restaurants near the office.
This restaurant is famous for bulgogi.
Is there a restaurant near here?

grammar: 뭐가 맛있어요? (mwoga masisseoyo = what's tasty?) — ask staff; they love recommending.

english: The pork belly here is really delicious.
grammar: 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal = pork belly) — 삼 (three) layers of meat and fat.

english: This place is famous for cold noodles.
grammar: 집 (jip = house) also means a go-to eatery: 냉면 집 = a naengmyeon place.
명 (myeong) counts people with native numbers: 두 명 (du myeong = two people).

english: Two servings of pork belly, please.
grammar: 인분 (inbun = serving) takes Sino numbers: 2인분 (i-inbun = two servings).
Ordering with 하나 (hana = one) after the dish name is the everyday pattern.
셀프 (selpeu = self-serve) — at many Korean restaurants you fetch water yourself.
반찬 (banchan = side dishes) come free — and usually refillable.
줄 (jul = roll/line) counts gimbap: 두 줄 (du jul = two rolls).

english: What are you going to order?
grammar: 시키다 (sikida = to order food): 뭐 시킬 거예요? = what'll you order?
도 (do = also) replaces 은/는/이/가: 밥도 = rice too.
저기요 (jeogiyo = excuse me) is the polite way to call restaurant staff.
마리 (mari) counts animals — and whole chickens on menus: 한 마리 (han mari).
병 (byeong = bottle) with native numbers: 한 병 (han byeong = one bottle).
Point and say 이거 주세요 (igeo juseyo = this one, please) — orders anything.

english: Cold noodles for me too, please.

grammar: 나오다 (naoda = to come out) is how Koreans say food arrives: 나왔어요.
맛이 어때요? (masi eottaeyo = how's the taste?) — 맛 (mat) = taste.

english: This kimchi stew is a bit spicy.
The chili pepper is really spicy.
grammar: 진짜 (jinjja = really) — the casual-but-polite cousin of 정말 (jeongmal).
너무 (neomu = too) turns praise into complaint: 너무 짜요 = too salty.

english: The broth really hits the spot!
grammar: 시원해요 (siwonhaeyo = refreshing) — Koreans say it even about hot soup that hits the spot.
뜨거워요 (tteugeowoyo) = hot to the touch; spicy-hot is 매워요 (maewoyo).

english: This side dish is a bit bland.
grammar: 싱거워요 (singgeowoyo = bland) — the opposite of 짜요 (jjayo = salty).
맛없어요 (madeopseoyo = tastes bad) — 맛 (taste) + 없다 (to not exist).

english: The food at that restaurant wasn't good.
The tteokbokki yesterday was really spicy.
The chicken is nice and crispy.
grammar: 치킨 (chikin) means fried chicken only; a live or raw chicken is 닭 (dak).

english: The cold noodles were so refreshing.
The taste is a little different.

grammar: 필요 없어요 (piryo eopseoyo = no need) — a polite "I'm good."
배불러요 (baebulleoyo = I'm full) — 배 (belly) + 부르다; say it after a good meal.
배달 (baedal = delivery) — in Korea almost anything arrives at your door.

english: Last night I had a late-night snack.
grammar: 야식 (yasik = late-night food) — a beloved Korean institution.

english: The food came thirty minutes later.
grammar: 후에 (hue = after): 삼십 분 후에 = thirty minutes later.

english: I ordered pizza on the app.
We're going to order Chinese food.

grammar: 그릇 (geureut = bowl) with native numbers: 두 그릇 (du geureut = two bowls).

english: How much is the delivery fee?
grammar: 비 (bi) on the end of a noun = fee: 배달비 (baedalbi = delivery fee).
Money uses Sino numbers: 삼천 원 (samcheon won = 3,000 won).

english: We're waiting for the delivery now.
Ramyeon is the best late-night food.
I drank every last drop of the broth.
grammar: 까지 (kkaji = even/up to): 국물까지 = even the broth.
계산서 (gyesanseo = the bill) — ask for it, or just pay at the counter.
돼요? (dwaeyo = does it work?) is the all-purpose "can I...?": 카드 돼요?

english: How much did it come to?
grammar: Bills "come out" in Korean: 얼마 나왔어요? (eolma nawasseoyo = how much is it?)
만 (man = 10,000) is the money unit: 사만 원 (saman won = 40,000 won).
계산하다 (gyesanhada = to pay the bill) — Koreans often insist on paying for the table.
사다 (sada = to buy) also means "to treat": 제가 살 거예요 = my treat!
No tipping needed in Korea: 팁이 없어요 (tibi eopseoyo).
괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) politely declines — a soft "no thanks."
내다 (naeda = to pay): 같이 냈어요 = we paid together.

english: Yesterday the company paid for dinner.
grammar: 값 (gap = cost) attaches to nouns: 저녁값 (jeonyeokgap = the dinner bill).
Past = ㅆ + 어요: 먹었어요 (meogeosseoyo = ate).
지난 (jinan = last): 지난 주말 (jinan jumal = last weekend).

english: On Friday we ate out as a family.
We had a company dinner yesterday.
grammar: 회식 (hoesik = team dinner) — after-work meals are big in Korean work life.

english: We grilled meat at the company dinner.
grammar: 굽다 (gupda = to grill) → 구워요 (guwoyo) — you grill at the table in Korea.

english: What did you have for lunch?
I tried soft-tofu stew for the first time.

grammar: 그래서 (geuraeseo = so/therefore) links a cause to what happened.

english: What are you going to eat tonight?
grammar: Future = -(으)ㄹ 거예요: 먹을 거예요 (meogeul geoyeyo = will eat).

english: Tomorrow I'm having lunch with a friend.
This weekend we'll try a new restaurant.
grammar: 새 (sae = new) sits before a noun: 새 식당 = a new restaurant.
파전 (pajeon = green-onion pancake) — Korea's favorite rainy-day food.

english: Tomorrow I'll have breakfast at home.
Next week I'm going to learn to cook.
Mom is going to make seaweed soup.
grammar: 미역국 (miyeokguk = seaweed soup) — the traditional Korean birthday breakfast.

english: We'll have cake on the birthday too.
So I'll prepare lots of food.
Do you take the subway to work?
grammar: 로 (ro = by) marks transport: 지하철로 (jihacheollo = by subway).

english: Yes, I ride the subway every day.

grammar: 호선 (hoseon = subway line) takes Sino numbers: 2호선 (i-hoseon = Line 2).

english: I get off at City Hall Station.
grammar: 내리다 (naerida = to get off): 역에서 내려요 = get off at the station.

english: I'll get off at the next station.

grammar: 갈아타요 (garatayo = transfer), from 갈아타다 — 갈아 (change) + 타다 (ride).

english: Do you have a T-money card?
grammar: 티머니 (T-money) — the tap card for subway, bus, and even taxis.

english: I top up my T-money at the convenience store.
grammar: 충전하다 (chungjeonhada = to top up/charge) — cards and phone batteries alike.

english: Yesterday I loaded 10,000 won onto it.
The subway is faster than the bus.
grammar: 보다 (boda) after a noun = than: 버스보다 빨라요 = faster than the bus.

english: At rush hour there are so many people.
grammar: 출근 (chulgeun = going to work): 출근 시간 = rush hour.

english: Is there a subway station around here?
What time is the last train?
grammar: 막차 (makcha = last train) — miss it and it's a taxi night.

english: I listen to music on the subway.

grammar: 정거장 (jeonggeojang) counts stops: 세 정거장 (se jeonggeojang = three stops).
번 (beon = number) takes Sino numbers: 273번 버스 = bus number 273.

english: Does this bus go to City Hall?
I missed the bus this morning.
The next bus comes in ten minutes.
grammar: 분 (bun = minute) takes Sino numbers: 10분 (sip bun = ten minutes).

english: The bus was way too crowded.
I waited five minutes at the stop.
How much is the bus fare?
grammar: 요금 (yogeum = fare) — bus, subway, and taxi all use this word.
찍다 (jjikda = to tap/stamp): 카드를 찍어요 = tap your card.

english: You tap your card on the bus too.
I'm going to catch a taxi.
grammar: 잡다 (japda = to catch): 택시를 잡아요 = hail a taxi.

english: I called a taxi with the app.
Is the fare to the airport expensive?

grammar: 막히다 (makida = to be blocked): 길이 막혀요 = the roads are jammed.
기사님 (gisanim) — 기사 (driver) + honorific 님; the polite address for drivers.

english: The subway is cheaper than a taxi.
Next month I'm going to Busan.
grammar: 다음 달 (daeum dal = next month) — 달 (moon) also means month.
예매하다 (yemaehada = to book ahead) — train, movie, and concert tickets.

english: I'm going from Seoul to Busan by train.
grammar: 에서...까지 (eseo...kkaji) = from...to: 서울에서 부산까지.

english: KTX tickets are a bit pricey.
I ate a boxed lunch on the train.
grammar: 도시락 (dosirak = boxed lunch) — a classic of Korean train rides.

english: The tickets are already sold out.
grammar: 매진 (maejin = sold out): 매진이에요 — you'll see it on booking screens.

english: So I bought a bus ticket.
The express bus is comfortable too.
I bought snacks at the rest stop.
grammar: 휴게소 (hyugeso = highway rest stop) — its snacks are a road-trip ritual.

english: The next train leaves at two.
grammar: 시 (si = o'clock) takes native numbers: 두 시 (du si = two o'clock).

english: We'll arrive at six in the evening.

grammar: 승강장 (seunggangjang = platform) — signs also say 타는 곳 (taneun got).
길을 잃어버렸어요 (gireul ireobeoryeosseoyo = I lost my way) — the traveler's essential.
(으)로 marks direction: 오른쪽으로 (oreunjjogeuro = to the right).
사거리 (sageori = intersection) — 사 (four) + 거리 (street): where four roads meet.
쭉 (jjuk = straight on): 쭉 가요 — usually with a hand pointing the way.

english: Cross the street in front of the bank.
It's next to the convenience store.

grammar: 건너편 (geonneopyeon = the far side): 카페 건너편 = across from the cafe.
Subway exits are numbered: 4번 출구 (sabeon chulgu = exit 4) — how Koreans set meeting spots.

english: I found the station on the map.
I asked a subway staff member.
grammar: 물어보다 (mureoboda = to ask): 길을 물어봤어요 = asked the way.

english: My friend sent me a map.

grammar: 이제 (ije = now, from now on) — for a change of state: 이제 알아요 = now I know.

english: How long does it take to your office?
grammar: 얼마나 걸려요? (eolmana geollyeoyo = how long does it take?) — THE commute question.

english: How long from here to the airport?

grammar: Sino numbers stack: 삼십 (samsip = thirty) = 삼 (3) × 십 (10).

english: It took longer than I expected.
grammar: 생각보다 (saenggakboda = than expected): 생각보다 오래 = longer than expected.

english: It takes an hour by plane.
grammar: 시간 (sigan = hours of duration) takes native numbers: 한 시간 (han sigan).
제주도 (Jejudo) — Korea's holiday island; Seoul–Jeju is the world's busiest air route.

english: I got to the airport two hours early.
It's a short trip from home to work.
Last year I traveled around Korea.
I saw the sea in Busan.
I went to Gyeongju by train.
I took lots of photos there.
grammar: 사진을 찍다 (sajineul jjikda = to take a photo) — same 찍다 as tapping a card!

english: The hotel was close to the station.
Last summer I went to Jeju.

grammar: 렌터카 (renteoka = rental car) — Konglish, straight from "rent-a-car".

english: I bought souvenirs at the market.
I sent the trip photos to my family.
grammar: 한테 (hante = to a person): 가족한테 보냈어요 = sent to my family.

english: I still can't forget that trip.
grammar: 못 (mot = can't) before the verb: 못 잊어요 = can't forget.

english: Next week I'm going on a trip.
grammar: 여행을 가다 (yeohaengeul gada = to go on a trip) — trips are "gone", not "made".

english: I'm going to Gangneung with a friend.
We'll book a hotel near the sea.
grammar: 예약 (yeyak) reserves places; 예매 (yemae) books tickets.

english: I'll buy the train tickets in advance.
On Jeju we'll go to Hallasan.
grammar: 산 (san = mountain): 한라산 (Hallasan) — Korea's tallest, on Jeju.
구경하다 (gugyeonghada = to sightsee/look around) — markets, palaces, anything.
Wear a 한복 (hanbok = traditional dress) and palace entry in Seoul is free.

english: We'll have dinner at the night market.
Where will you go on vacation?
grammar: 때 (ttae = the time of): 휴가 때 (hyuga ttae = during vacation).

english: I'm going to travel around Europe.
I'm going to make a travel plan.
grammar: Plans are "built" in Korean: 계획을 세워요 (gyehoegeul sewoyo = make a plan).
